name: Hezekiah
role: King of Judah who trusted the LORD against Assyria
whenBasis: The reign as the Reign tab dates it, from Thiele's reconstruction of the kings' stated lengths and synchronisms; the other readings there differ by a few years.
summary: Son of Ahaz, who did right like David: he removed the high places, broke the sacred pillars, and smashed the bronze serpent Moses had made, because the people burned incense to it. He rebelled against Assyria; Sennacherib took Judah's fortified cities and besieged Jerusalem, and Hezekiah spread the Assyrian letter before the LORD. The angel of the LORD struck the Assyrian camp. Sick to the point of death, he prayed and was given fifteen more years, then showed his treasures to envoys from Babylon.
body: Kings says he trusted in the LORD as no king of Judah before or after him. Chronicles adds that he reopened and cleansed the temple and held a great Passover, inviting the remnant of the north. He paid Sennacherib tribute, stripping the gold from the temple doors, but the Assyrians still came. Their commander's taunts are carried to him; Isaiah answers that the king of Assyria will not enter the city or shoot an arrow there.

When Isaiah tells him to put his house in order, he turns his face to the wall and weeps. The LORD adds fifteen years, and the shadow goes back ten steps on the stairway of Ahaz as a sign. When he shows the Babylonian envoys everything in his storehouses, Isaiah foretells that all of it will be carried to Babylon. He also made the pool and the tunnel that brought water into the city.

moments.text: Removes the high places and Nehushtan
Spreads the letter before the LORD

later.text: Sennacherib's own annals, on the Taylor Prism (British Museum 91032) and the Oriental Institute Prism, claim he took forty-six of Hezekiah's walled cities and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem “like a bird in a cage,” and list his tribute; they do not claim to have taken the city.

sources.title: Oriental Institute Prism of Sennacherib, Chicago, A2793

later.text: An inscription found in 1880 in the tunnel from the Gihon spring to the Siloam pool tells how the two teams of diggers met. The tunnel is usually identified as Hezekiah's.
A clay seal impression reading “belonging to Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah” was found in the Ophel excavations in Jerusalem in 2009 and published in 2015.

sources.title: Bulla of Hezekiah, Ophel excavations, Jerusalem
